standard.title: Develop system investigation questions
standard.description: develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4S01 (Develop guided investigation questions): Students develop questions to guide investigations of people, events, places and communities with teacher support. Students have practised formulating basic investigation questions in Year 4.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop a range of purposeful questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems, selecting question types appropriate to the inquiry purpose and disciplinary focus.

nodes.label: Question types and purposes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between different types of questions used in HASS inquiry (probing, open-ended, practical, financial) and explain the purpose of each type.
nodes.minimum_width: Name two types of inquiry questions and explain when each is most useful.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the range of question types used in HASS inquiry: probing questions (to seek specific details), open-ended questions (to elicit ideas and multiple perspectives), and practical questions (to guide action, financial choices or investigation logistics); explain when each type is appropriate.
wider: Explore how question type selection varies across HASS disciplines — compare the questions a historian uses with those a geographer or economist would use for the same event or phenomenon
Investigate how disciplinary concepts (history, geography, economics, civics) should shape question design — and practice generating questions that frame inquiry from a specific disciplinary angle
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish question types will default to closed factual questions for all inquiry stages. Understanding that different question types serve different stages and purposes is foundational for purposeful investigation across HASS disciplines.

response_modes.reason: Use a question classification exercise — sort sample questions into types and explain the purpose of each. Model question design explicitly before students write their own.

success_criteria: Students name at least two question types and explain the purpose of each.
Students give an example of a question from each type they name.

nodes.label: Framing inquiry questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop questions that address relevant disciplinary concepts and frame the stages of an inquiry, from initial investigation through to conclusions.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least three questions that frame a HASS inquiry from start to finish, using at least two different question types.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a set of inquiry questions that address relevant disciplinary concepts, frame investigation stages (before, during, after), and include probing, open-ended and practical question types appropriate to the inquiry topic.
wider: Develop inquiry questions for a multi-disciplinary HASS topic (e.g. combining historical, geographic and economic angles on colonial settlement) that reveal connections across disciplines
Refine an initial set of inquiry questions based on preliminary research — modelling the iterative nature of professional inquiry

response_modes.reason: Question design improves through practice across multiple topics. Build a bank of strong inquiry questions that students can use as models — diversity of examples is more valuable than perfecting a single question set.

success_criteria: Students develop at least three questions that together frame a HASS inquiry.
Students use at least two different question types and explain why each is appropriate for its stage of inquiry.

nodes.label: Questions to locate and evaluate sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop practical questions to identify, locate and evaluate sources useful for an investigation, including questions about source usefulness, reliability and access.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop two questions to guide the identification or evaluation of sources for an investigation.
nodes.typical_width: Develop practical questions to guide source location and evaluation: 'Is this source useful?', 'Who can help with this project?', 'What protocols must be followed for this inquiry?', 'What resources do we need?' — and explain the purpose of each question in the investigation process.
wider: Develop a source evaluation checklist framed as a set of questions, and apply it to evaluate the usefulness of several different source types for the same inquiry
Explore how the questions posed at the start of an inquiry shape which sources are sought — and how finding unexpected sources can prompt new questions

response_modes.reason: Source-evaluation questions are best practised across a range of source types (primary, secondary, digital, oral) — each type raises different evaluative questions. Breadth of source types matters more than depth on one.

success_criteria: Students develop at least two questions designed to locate or evaluate sources for an inquiry.
Students explain how answering these questions would improve their investigation.

nodes.label: Developing a complete inquiry question set
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a complete set of purposeful questions for a HASS inquiry that spans investigation stages, addresses relevant disciplinary concepts, and guides source selection and action.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a set of at least four questions for a HASS inquiry that cover different stages and purposes.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a complete inquiry question set for a HASS topic that: frames initial investigation, probes for detail, guides source selection, and leads toward conclusions and action; addresses relevant disciplinary concepts; and uses a range of question types appropriate to their purpose.
wider: Evaluate the quality of a question set by testing it against a completed inquiry — assess which questions were most valuable and revise questions that did not generate useful inquiry

Develop questions that connect multiple HASS disciplines to explore a complex topic (e.g. 'How do purchasing decisions affect the environment and community?' — connecting economics, geography and civics)

response_modes.reason: A complete inquiry question set requires students to coordinate all question types across all stages of inquiry — the integration challenge is designing a coherent sequence, not just a list of questions.

success_criteria: Students develop at least four inquiry questions that cover different stages and purposes.
Students use at least two distinct question types and explain the role of each in their inquiry.
Questions address relevant HASS disciplinary concepts rather than generic factual queries.
